The Pale-legged leaf warbler (Phylloscopus tenellipes) is a small migratory passerine that breeds in the understory of mixed coniferous and deciduous forests across northeastern Asia. At hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge weighing just 1.2 grams [Ww0 = 1.2 grams], a remarkably low initial mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves typical of insectivorous passerines. Egg incubation under natural nest conditions, which maintain an average temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], proceeds for an incubation period lasting approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days]. This period of embryonic development is relatively brief compared to many temperate-zone warblers, likely an adaptation to the short breeding season at higher latitudes. Following hatching, the nestlings undergo rapid somatic growth, consuming protein-rich invertebrate prey delivered frequently by both parents. The accelerated growth trajectory is essential for achieving the developmental milestones required before the onset of the autumn migration. Field studies have documented that the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of about 8.2 years [am = about 8.2 years], determined through recapture records of banded individuals, though most free-living birds survive for considerably shorter durations due to predation and migratory h at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]azards.

Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of an actively foraging adult, measured at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the basal metabolic rate of Phylloscopus tenellipes has been recorded at 28.94 milliliters per hour [JOi = 28.94 milliliters per hour]. This relatively modest metabolic rate is consistent with the general pattern observed among small-bodied Phylloscopus warblers, which maintain high energetic demands to support their active insectivorous foraging strategy. The reproductive output of the species is constrained by the brevity of the temperate breeding season. Females typically lay a single clutch containing five to six eggs per clutch [N_R_i = five to six eggs per clutch], and they produce only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], resulting in a modest annual fecundity. This single-brooded strategy is common among long-distance migratory passerines that must complete nesting, fledging, and post-breeding molt within a narrow temporal window before departure for southern wintering grounds. The absolute timing of these reproductive events is closely tied to local phenology, particularly the peak emergence of lepidopteran larvae, which constitutes the primary food source for provisioning nestlings.

Sexual maturation in the Pale-legged leaf warbler occurs at a relatively consistent age under the thermal regimes characteristic of its breeding habitat, where ambient temperatures during the active season average approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] for metabolically active individuals. Puberty is attained at 31.5 days after hatching [tp = 31.5 days after hatching], an interval that coincides with the completion of juvenile feather development and the achievement of near-adult body mass at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid onset of reproductive maturity is typical of short-lived passerines that must maximize lifetime reproductive output within a small number of breeding seasons. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, young birds do not immediately initiate breeding; instead, a significant delay occurs before the first reproductive attempt. The time since birth at first brood is exactly 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], meaning that individuals hatched in one summer will not breed until the following spring, approximately one year later at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This obligatory delay reflects the necessity for first-year birds to complete a full migratory cycle and establish a breeding territory before engaging in reproduction. The pronounced seasonality of the temperate environment constrains the timing of first breeding to the subsequent breeding season following hatching.

The fledging period represents a critical developmental transition for nestling warblers, marking the shift from a stationary, brooded existence within the nest to an active, mobile lifestyle in the surrounding vegetation. Under the elevated body temperature typical of endothermic chicks, which maintain a core temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 10.5 days [tx = 10.5 days]. This rapid fledging interval, lasting between 10 and 11 days post-hatching, is characteristic of many Phylloscopus species and reflects the selective pressure to minimize nest predation risk by shortening the vulnerable nestling stage. Upon leaving the nest, fledglings remain dependent on parental provisioning for an additional period while they refine their foraging skills and develop flight proficiency. The accelerated pace of early development is facilitated by the high-quality insect diet provided by both parents, which delivers sufficient energy to sustain both rapid feather growth and the high metabolic demands of thermoregulation. Body mass increases dramatically during this nestling phase, culminating in the adult size that will support the demanding migratory flights ahead.

Adult body size in Phylloscopus tenellipes displays a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a smaller asymptotic mass compared to males. The ultimate wet weight for females is 8.6 grams [Wwi = 8.6 grams], while the ultimate wet weight for males reaches a substantially larger 11.8 grams [Wwi = 11.8 grams]. This degree of dimorphism, with males being approximately 37 percent heavier than females, is notable among warblers and may arise from sexual selection acting on male body size during territory establishment and courtship displays. The larger body mass in males likely confers advantages in competitive interactions for high-quality breeding territories, which in turn influences reproductive success. In contrast, the smaller body size of females may reduce energetic demands during the egg-laying and incubation periods, allowing greater allocation of resources to clutch production. Both sexes, however, exhibit a moderate body mass that falls within the typical range for members of the genus Phylloscopus, a group characterized by small, insectivorous, and highly active species. The intersexual difference in mass is consistent across populations, suggesting a stable evolutionary trajectory shaped by differences in the selective pressures acting on each sex.
